title: Japan Has Been Here Before: The 1987 Persian Gulf Crisis
author: TSURUTA Jun
text:
TOKYO, JAPAN – MAY 4TH 2016. JS 302 Tsushima Yaeyama-class minesweeper is open to the public in Tokyo Bay. The Tsushima was commisioned in 1993.
Credit: Keith Tarrier / Shutterstock
The Strait of Hormuz was effectively closed following the U.S. and Israeli attacks on Iran in February, leaving oil tankers unable to transit the strait, which is both the entrance to the Persian Gulf and one of the world’s most critical trade arteries. Japan imports more than 90 percent of its crude oil from the Middle East. Gasoline prices have surged, and the effects on daily life have been wide-ranging. The current crisis has a precedent. During the Iran-Iraq War of the 1980s, the Japanese government actively debated whether to send Maritime Self-Defense Force (MSDF) minesweepers and Japan Coast Guard (JCG) patrol vessels to the Persian Gulf — and ultimately chose not to.Iraq invaded Iran in September 1980, beginning the Iran–Iraq War. Around 1984 the conflict spread to the sea, and passage through the Persian Gulf became hazardous for tankers as missile attacks and mines proliferated. In July 1987, at Kuwait’s request, the U.S. government dispatched warships and began escorting tankers, but a tanker still struck a mine. Washington then asked Western countries, including Japan, to send minesweepers. The U.K., France, Italy, the Netherlands, and Belgium all subsequently contributed to the minesweeping effort.[...]
